title: How a bicycle stays upright

parts.label: Front wheel
parts.brief: A thin road bicycle wheel standing upright in the x-y plane with its axle along z. It has a black rubber tyre with a fine tread around a silver aluminium rim. Thirty-two thin silver spokes run from the rim to a small round hub in the centre, with a short axle sticking out on each side.

parts.label: Rear wheel
parts.brief: A thin bicycle wheel standing upright in the x-y plane with its axle along z. It has a black rubber tyre with a fine tread around a silver aluminium rim. Thirty-two thin silver spokes meet a hub that has a small stack of toothed silver gears (the cassette) on one side.

parts.label: Saddle
parts.brief: A narrow bicycle seat seen from the side, long front-to-back along x. It has a black padded top with a pointed nose toward +x and a wider rounded back. Underneath are two thin silver rails that clamp onto the top of the seat post.

parts.label: Pedals and chainring
parts.brief: A round silver chainring with about 40 small pointed teeth around its edge, standing upright in the x-y plane. A short black crank arm sits on each side, and the two arms point in opposite directions. At the end of each crank arm is a flat black pedal with a grippy edge, sticking out sideways along z.

steps.say: This is a bicycle. Stand it alone and it falls right over. But give it a push, and it can roll along by itself without tipping! Let's find out how.
First, the wheels. A bicycle only balances when it is moving. The faster the wheels roll, the steadier the bike feels. Standing still, it has no tricks to use at all.

Here is the big secret: steering. When the bike starts to lean left, the front wheel turns left too. That swings the wheels back underneath the bike, like moving your hand to keep a broom balanced on your palm.

Look inside the head tube. The fork turns in there, and it is tilted, not straight up and down. Because of this tilt, the tyre touches the ground a little behind where the steering line points, just like the wheel on a shopping cart.
That shopping cart trick means the front wheel steers itself. When the bike leans, the wheel gets pulled to turn into the lean all on its own, catching the fall before you even notice.

The frame holds it all in the right shape: the top tube, down tube, seat tube and the stays out to the back wheel. The pedals and chainring keep the bike moving, and moving is what lets the steering trick work.
Now everything comes back together. Rolling wheels plus a tilted fork that steers into every wobble: that is how a moving bicycle keeps itself upright!

recap: A moving bicycle stays up because its tilted front fork steers the wheel into any lean, putting the wheels back under the bike.
question: Have you ever noticed your handlebars turning a little by themselves when you start to wobble?
